records.place: Illmitz, in the Seewinkel on the eastern shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Kracher Trockenbeerenauslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein: Trockenbeerenauslese, from shrivelled, botrytised berries of at least 30 degrees KMW
wine.grapes: Welschriesling, Chardonnay, Scheurebe, Traminer and Muskat Ottonel, and Zweigelt in some years; most numbered wines are of one grape, the Grande Cuvée a blend.
wine.sites: Flat vineyards between Illmitz and the shore of the shallow Neusiedlersee, where autumn mists off the water bring noble rot almost every year.
wine.making: The year's botrytised wines are kept apart, each mostly of one grape. No sugar may be added: the sweetness is the grape's own, left when the fermentation stops. Zwischen den Seen wines are raised in steel tanks or large wooden casks for clear fruit, Nouvelle Vague wines in new barriques. Since 1995 every Trockenbeerenauslese of the year has been numbered, the denser the wine, the higher its number.
wine.glass: Glazed pineapple, candied lemon and mango over honey in the Zwischen den Seen wines, with the toast and vanilla of new oak in the Nouvelle Vague; luscious and dense, yet lifted by fresh acidity, and long.
wine.ageing: Open and fruity on release, it keeps for decades, the fruit slowly giving way to honey, dried apricot and toffee.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, and small pours.

label.means: Prädikatswein from shrivelled, botrytised berries of at least 30 degrees KMW, never sweetened or chaptalised.
The wine's place in that year's collection: the denser the wine, the higher the number, by the house's own account.
Between the lakes: the line raised in steel tanks or large wooden casks, for pure fruit.
New wave: the line raised in new barriques, the Grande Cuvée among them.

records.table: Weinlaubenhof Kracher, at Illmitz by the Neusiedlersee, numbers each year's Trockenbeerenauslesen, the denser the wine the higher the number. The Welschriesling from steel or large casks gives glazed pineapple and honey, while the Nouvelle Vague wines take the toast of new oak.
records.story: The estate began as a small mixed farm at Illmitz, in the Seewinkel; the house says its farmer had long wanted to make wine, and in 1959 the winery was founded. That same year his son, Alois Kracher (1959 to 2007), was born. Trained as a chemist, the son began working beside his father in 1981, at twenty two, and turned the estate towards the botrytised sweet wines that the lake's autumn mists make possible. In the years after the diethylene glycol scandal of 1985, which had wrecked the name of Austria's sweet wines abroad, the Kracher wines went out into the world, and in the house's telling the 1991 vintage made their name. From 1995, by the house's reckoning, every Trockenbeerenauslese of a year was numbered, the denser the wine the higher its number, each in one of two lines, Zwischen den Seen or Nouvelle Vague. Alois Kracher died of cancer in December 2007, at forty eight, and his son took the estate on. A run of Kracher numbers on a list is a lesson in botrytis at one sitting: grape against grape, steel against new oak, and the number telling how dense each wine will be.

others.name: Grande Cuvée Trockenbeerenauslese
others.note: A blend of Chardonnay and Welschriesling, raised in new barriques and numbered among the Nouvelle Vague wines.

others.name: Beerenauslese Cuvée
others.note: Welschriesling and Chardonnay at Beerenauslese ripeness, the lighter way into the house's sweet wines.

others.name: Auslese Cuvée
others.note: Welschriesling and Chardonnay at Auslese ripeness, and lighter again.

traps: The numbers rank density within one vintage, the higher the denser; they are no measure of quality, and the No. 7 of one year is not the No. 7 of another.
Zwischen den Seen and Nouvelle Vague name the vessel and the style, steel or large casks against new barriques, not the sweetness or the site.
Welschriesling is no relation of Riesling, and no Illmitz wine is ever an Ausbruch, a name kept for Rust across the lake.

cards.front: Kracher: from which vintage has every Trockenbeerenauslese of the year carried a number?
cards.back: 1995, as the house dates it: the denser the wine, the higher the number.

cards.front: Which Kracher line is raised in new barriques, and which in steel tanks or large casks?
cards.back: Nouvelle Vague in new barriques; Zwischen den Seen in steel tanks or large wooden casks.

questions.q: A guest compares two Kracher Trockenbeerenauslesen of one vintage, No. 3 and No. 9. What does the higher number tell the guest?
opts: The wine is denser and sweeter
The wine has spent longer in bottle
The grapes grew on a higher slope
The wine is judged the better of the two
questions.exp: The house numbers each year's Trockenbeerenauslesen by density, the higher the denser and sweeter; the number ranks no quality, and the No. 9 is no older than the No. 3.

questions.q: Alois Kracher joined his father's estate at Illmitz in 1981, at twenty two. What had he trained as?
opts: A chemist
A cooper
A banker
A chef
questions.exp: He trained as a chemist and then turned the family estate to botrytised sweet wine; the estate itself had begun in 1959 as a small mixed farm, not a cooperage.

report: The library record w-kracher-tba and its trap say the numbers identify lots and are no sweetness scale; the house's own definitions page says the denser the wine, the higher its number, as Vinography and a second guide also report, so the record follows the house and the library line should change.

The library has Zwischen den Seen in large neutral cask and the region record's producers line has it in steel; the house says steel tanks or large wooden casks with long lees contact, which the record keeps.
Founded 1959 rests on the house's own history page; the founder, born in 1928 or 1929 by differing accounts and dead in 2010, is described rather than named.

The appellation is given as Burgenland; since the 2020 vintage a Trockenbeerenauslese of the area may also be labelled Neusiedlersee DAC Reserve (Austrian Wine), and whether recent Kracher labels use it was not confirmed.
Left out for want of a second source: the comparative tastings against Château d'Yquem in 1988 and 1993 (one encyclopaedia only) and the renaming of a sweet wine trophy after Alois Kracher in 2008.
Alois Kracher's son, who took over in 2007, is living and is not named; he is already in people.json.

wine.sites: the salt pans of the Seewinkel are cut, found in no source of this check; the house's own pages place the vineyards between Illmitz and the shore of the lake.

wine.making: the long lees contact of the Zwischen den Seen wines is cut, since the house's pages describe that line by its vessel alone, steel tanks or large wooden casks; the numbering is dated from 1995, as the house gives it.

wine.label: Nouvelle Vague no longer claims a debt to the French films of the 1950s, which no source gave; it now names the Grande Cuvée among the wines raised in new barriques, as the house's own review page and a merchant give it.

story: the son began working beside his father in 1981, at twenty two, no longer simply joined the estate, since the encyclopaedia has him part time from 1981 and full time from 1986; the 1991 vintage that made the wines' name is told as the house's account, since another account dates the breakthrough to 1995; then in his twenties is cut for want of a source.

others: the Grande Cuvée is a blend of Chardonnay and Welschriesling raised in new barriques among the Nouvelle Vague wines, as two vintages' listings and the house's review page give it, no longer only a blend.

records.place: Rust, on the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Ruster Ausbruch
wine.classification: Prädikatswein at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness, at least 30 degrees KMW, from Rust alone
wine.grapes: White grapes of Rust, the grape or the blend changing with the bottling: Weissburgunder, Chardonnay, Welschriesling, Pinot Gris, Neuburger and Gelber Muskateller among them.
wine.sites: Vineyards within the town limits of Rust, on limestone and schist sloping gently down to the western shore of the lake, whose autumn mists bring noble rot; the Ried Oberer Wald gives one bottling of its own.
wine.making: The shrivelled, botrytised berries are picked by hand, broken out of the bunch, which, the house explains, gives Ausbruch its name, and every grape must grow within the town limits of Rust. Nothing may be added to sweeten it. Recent bottlings are raised in barriques, new in part for the Pinot Cuvée and used for the Essenz; some older vintages were raised partly in steel.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, orange peel and honey, with the faint toast of a used barrique; rich and sweet but never syrupy, its fresh acidity carrying it a long way.
wine.ageing: Charming young for its apricot fruit, which over decades in bottle turns slowly to dried fruit, toffee and honey.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, poured from the bottle without decanting, in small measures and a small glass, beside blue cheese or an apricot tart.

label.means: From the 2020 vintage, Rust's own appellation, reserved for sweet wine from botrytised, naturally shrivelled berries grown in the town.
Wine of a Prädikat, picked ripe and never chaptalised or sweetened: its sweetness is the grape's own.
A blend of Weissburgunder and Chardonnay, with Pinot Gris and Neuburger in some years.

records.table: Feiler-Artinger keeps Rust's old sweet wine alive in a baroque house on the town's main street: Ruster Ausbruch, honeyed and full of candied apricot yet fresh, made from botrytised berries broken out of the bunch by hand.
records.story: Rust, on the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, has lived by sweet wine for five centuries. In June 1524 Mary of Hungary (1505 to 1558) granted its growers the right to burn an R into their casks, and in 1681, as Austrian Wine tells it, the town bought its charter as a royal free town from Emperor Leopold I (1640 to 1705) for sixty thousand gulden and five hundred pails of Ausbruch. In 1936 a couple of the Feiler family bought a baroque burgher's house at Hauptstrasse 3, in the old centre, and made wine there; the husband first bottled it in 1947, and in 1953, on the house's own word, he made Ruster Ausbruch again after the war. The next generation ran the estate with a sister of the family, and in the middle 1980s, as the glycol scandal of 1985 shook Austria's sweet wine, her married name, Artinger, joined Feiler's on the label. In 2016 the law reserved the word Ausbruch to Rust, and from the 2020 vintage Ruster Ausbruch DAC became, in Austrian Wine's words, the country's first origin protected for sweet wine alone, picked at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness. Feiler-Artinger's Ausbruch puts to rest a question every candidate meets: a place, not a technique, and Rust's own.

others.name: Ruster Ausbruch DAC Essenz
others.note: The densest bottling, very sweet and low in alcohol, raised for twenty months and more in used barriques.

others.name: Solitaire
others.note: The house's red blend: Blaufränkisch with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon.

traps: Ausbruch is Rust's alone: an Illmitz or Seewinkel sweet wine of the same ripeness is a Trockenbeerenauslese, never an Ausbruch.
Rust lies on the lake's western shore beside the Leithaberg; Illmitz and the Seewinkel lie across the water to the east.
Ausbruch once sat between Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese; from the 2020 vintage Ruster Ausbruch DAC is picked at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness.

cards.front: Feiler-Artinger: when did the family buy its baroque house in Rust, and when did it first bottle wine?
cards.back: It bought the house at Hauptstrasse 3 in 1936 and first bottled its wine in 1947.

cards.front: Where does the word Ausbruch come from, as Feiler-Artinger explains it?
cards.back: From the shrivelled berries broken out of the bunch by hand at harvest.

questions.q: Feiler-Artinger may label its sweet wine Ruster Ausbruch, while an Illmitz estate of the same ripeness may not. Why?
opts: The name is reserved to grapes grown in Rust
Only Furmint may be used for an Ausbruch
An Ausbruch must age ten years in cask
Only a growers' club may use the word
questions.exp: Since the law of 2016 and the DAC of 2020, Ausbruch is Rust's alone, from botrytised grapes grown in the town and picked by hand. No single grape is required, so Furmint is not the reason.

questions.q: In 1681 Rust bought its charter as a royal free town from Emperor Leopold I. What did it pay, as Austrian Wine tells it?
opts: Gulden and pails of Ausbruch
A fleet of boats for the lake
Its vineyards on the Leithaberg
A tithe of its grain harvest
questions.exp: The town paid sixty thousand gulden and five hundred pails of Ausbruch. The privilege of branding its casks with an R came earlier, in 1524, from Mary of Hungary.

report: The library lists Furmint among the grapes of the house's Ruster Ausbruch; no source found here names Furmint for Feiler-Artinger, so the record names the grapes the house's vintage pages and Falstaff's entries give (Weissburgunder, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Welschriesling, Neuburger).
Founded is left empty: the house dates its roots to the purchase of the house at Hauptstrasse 3 in 1936 and its founding to the 1930s, and a purchase is not a founding.

The founding couple and the second generation are described, not named, as no dates were found for the dead and the rest are living; the 1947 first bottling rests on two merchants' histories (Cavetta, Walters Feine Weine), the 1953 Ausbruch on the house and both merchants, and 1985 on Falstaff and the Burgenland Vinothek.

The vessels change with the bottling and the vintage: the house's recent sheets give used barriques, Falstaff's entries give barrique, partial barrique with steel, or steel, so the record says recent bottlings and some older vintages.
The 1993 Ruster Ausbruch's trophy at the International Wine Challenge in 1995, told on the house's site, is left out as an award.
Several dates of the second generation's taking over differ between merchants (1955, 1963, 1965) and are left out.

The privilege of 1524 rests on Austrian Wine and on the town of Rust's own anniversary material, whose Latin charter is dated 27 June 1524; the 1681 charter and its price on Austrian Wine and the Burgenländische Heimatblätter.

changed: wine.grapes: Weissburgunder is no longer said to lead; the grapes are listed without rank, Gelber Muskateller added, since Falstaff's entries show a Welschriesling Ausbruch, a Gelber Muskateller Ausbruch and Weissburgunder Essenzen, and the house's vintage page names Ruländer, Welschriesling, Weissburgunder and Neuburger.

wine.making, cards[0], questions[0]: the wine is no longer said to be pressed, raised and bottled in Rust; Austrian Wine and the federal product specification require the grapes to grow in Rust and be picked by hand, and the specification allows making outside the area with the regional committee's consent, so the card, the key and the explanation now ask where the grapes grow and how they are picked.

wine.making: the vessels are barriques, new in part for the Pinot Cuvée, as the house's own product page and a merchant give it, and used for the Essenz, as Falstaff's entries give it, no longer used barriques for every recent bottling; the Essenz's close to two years on its fine lees is cut, one vintage only and the lees found nowhere.

wine.label: the Pinot Cuvée is Weissburgunder and Chardonnay, with Pinot Gris and Neuburger in some years, as the house's product page for 2022 and an older listing give it, no longer the Pinot grapes with Chardonnay only in some years.

story: the double name no longer dates from 1985, in the very year of the glycol scandal; the house's own history gives 1986, on its founder's retirement, while the Burgenland Vinothek and Falstaff give 1985, so the story says the middle 1980s, as the scandal of 1985 shook Austria's sweet wine.

others: the Essenz's figures for alcohol and sugar, true of single vintages on Falstaff alone, give way to very sweet and low in alcohol, raised for twenty months and more in used barriques; Solitaire is Blaufränkisch with Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, as Falstaff, a Swiss merchant and an American listing give it, no longer the Bordeaux grapes in general.
questions[1]: the key's gold gulden becomes gulden, since the town's own page gives gulden and the Heimatblätter of 1927 give gold thalers.
open: Neuburger in the Ausbruch stands on the house's own vintage page alone; Furmint appears in one summary of the estate's grapes, so the library's Furmint is neither confirmed by two sources nor refuted, and the record leaves it out.
The Ried Oberer Wald bottling stands on one Falstaff entry and the author's reading.
The year of the double name, 1985 or 1986, is unsettled between the house and two secondary sources.

records.place: Lutzmannsburg in Mittelburgenland, with the cellar at Grosshöflein, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Lutzmannsburg Alte Reben
wine.sites: A selection of the house's oldest vines at Lutzmannsburg, in the south of Mittelburgenland, the eldest about a century old: sand, clay and loam, partly over limestone, on a plateau the house describes as an ancient volcano.
wine.making: Fermented on native yeasts in open wooden vats, about three weeks on the skins, then aged for about twenty months on its fine lees in large, used oak casks and bottled without fining or filtration, so that no new oak shows.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and blackberry with cracked black pepper and violet; rounder and darker than the Neckenmarkt, yet fine boned and savoury, with bright acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after five or so and keeps for two decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter suits a young bottle; a Burgundy glass, for its perfume.

label.means: Old vines: here a selection of the house's oldest at Lutzmannsburg, picked parcel by parcel.
The village in the south of Mittelburgenland where the vines grow.
The broad origin of the federal state, rather than the Mittelburgenland DAC in which the village lies.

records.table: Moric ferments its Blaufränkisch Lutzmannsburg Alte Reben, from the house's oldest vines in the south of Mittelburgenland, with native yeasts in open wooden vats, then rests it in large used casks rather than new oak. It is dark cherry and black pepper, savoury and fine.
records.story: Moric, said MO-ritz, dates from the 2001 vintage. Its maker came from the Velich family of Apetlon, in the Seewinkel, whose estate, Weingut Velich, is a separate house. Through the 1990s much Austrian red wine had chased weight, with long extraction and new barriques, and Moric went the other way. Its founder took on old Blaufränkisch vines, many on long leases and some about a century old, at Neckenmarkt in the north of Mittelburgenland and at Lutzmannsburg in the south, to compare what each village's soil and air gave the one grape, and took the fruit to a cellar at Grosshöflein on the Leithaberg. There the wines ferment with their own yeasts in open wooden vats and rest in large used casks for as long as they need, so that the vineyard speaks rather than the oak. With the 2005 vintage Mittelburgenland became a DAC for Blaufränkisch alone, yet the Lutzmannsburg is labelled simply Burgenland. Lutzmannsburg, on a plateau of sand, clay and loam partly over limestone, gives the rounder, darker wine; Neckenmarkt, on steep slopes of slate and limestone, the tauter one. Poured side by side, the two Alte Reben are the argument Moric makes: one grape, two villages, two wines.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Neckenmarkt Alte Reben
others.note: Old vines on steep slopes of slate and limestone, the tauter, more structured of the pair.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Burgenland
others.note: The entry Blaufränkisch, labelled simply Burgenland, that carries the house's reading of the grape.

traps: Moric is a separate house from Weingut Velich of Apetlon, though the two spring from one family.
Lutzmannsburg lies inside Mittelburgenland, yet Moric's wine is labelled Burgenland, not Mittelburgenland DAC.
Zweigelt is a crossing of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, never another name for Blaufränkisch.

Vine ages differ by source (80 to 100, 85 to 110, over 100); the record says eighty years and more, some over a century old.

The soil at Lutzmannsburg is sandy clay over a limestone base on an old volcanic plateau in the house's own material and a merchant's; the library says heavier clay, which agrees in part. Vinography puts the villages about ten kilometres apart and the house about twenty, so no distance is given.
The library's style line speaks of pale colour; Lutzmannsburg is the darker, rounder of the pair in the library's own wine list and in Vinography, which the glass follows.
The share of whole bunches rests on the library record alone; open wooden vats and about twenty months in old oak rest on one merchant and are left out.
No source found here explains the name Moric, so the story gives only its sound.

records.place: Rust, in the hills above the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental
wine.sites: The Ried Mariental at Rust: lean limestone soil, a microclimate of its own and very old vines, as the house describes it; the family's Oberer Wald, an inherited site whose rows run north to south, gives a cooler, slimmer wine.
wine.making: After fermentation on its skins, it spends close to two years in small oak barrels ahead of bottling; it is a dense, oak framed Blaufränkisch, built to be cellared rather than drunk young.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, blackberry and plum over cedar and cocoa, with a stony edge; firm, fine grained tannin and fresh acidity carry the oak to a long, taut finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and marked by oak when young, it needs about ten years to settle and lasts for twenty and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The named single vineyard at Rust, of lean limestone soil, that gives the wine its name.
The free town on the lake's western shore, the village named on the label.
The grape, called Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany.

records.table: Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental grows on lean limestone soil at Rust, and its 1986 vintage opened a new chapter for Austrian red wine. Close to two years in small oak barrels make it firm and dark, so give it ten years.
records.story: Like Rust's other growers, who have made sweet Ausbruch for centuries, the Triebaumers made it too, but their name travels on a dry red. In 1976, as the house tells it, a Rust couple who felt they lacked the equipment to do justice to their plot in the Mariental sold it to the family. Its lean limestone soil, its microclimate and its very old Blaufränkisch vines suited a red to keep. The 1986 Blaufränkisch Mariental came only a year after the diethylene glycol affair of 1985 had left Austrian wine's name abroad in ruins, and the house recalls that it had won almost every tasting it entered by 1988; Falstaff dates a new era of Austrian red wine from it. In later vintages the wine has spent close to two years in small oak barrels, a firmer frame than the large casks of much Austrian Blaufränkisch. Beside it the family bottles the Oberer Wald, a site it inherited, whose rows run north to south, as a slimmer, cooler counterpart. Austria's modern Blaufränkisch is usually told from one vintage, the Mariental of 1986.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Oberer Wald
others.note: An inherited site whose rows run north to south: a cooler, slimmer Blaufränkisch.

others.name: Ruster Ausbruch
others.note: The town's sweet wine from botrytised, shrivelled berries, made by the house beside its reds.

traps: Several Triebaumer estates make wine in Rust; the Mariental of 1986 is the Ernst Triebaumer estate's, so read the full name on the label.
Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany are Blaufränkisch by other names, whereas Zweigelt, its offspring, is a grape of its own.
The Mariental spends close to two years in small oak barrels, not in the large casks of much modern Blaufränkisch.

cards.front: Which vintage of Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental marked a turning point for Austrian red wine?
cards.back: 1986, the year after the glycol scandal.

cards.front: Ernst Triebaumer's Ried Mariental at Rust: what kind of soil does the house say it has?
cards.back: Lean limestone soil, with a microclimate of its own and very old vines.

questions.q: How is Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental aged before it is bottled?

Six months in stainless steel only
Four years in large old casks
A year in concrete eggs
questions.exp: The Mariental rests close to two years in small oak barrels; large old casks are the way of other Blaufränkisch, not of this one.

It was a gift of the Esterházy princes
The family planted it on cleared forest
It came with a house on the main street

report: The library's style line says the Mariental is made without heavy oak; wein.plus and a merchant say it spends close to two years in barrels of about three hundred litres, mostly new, and the record follows them, so the library line should change.
The library calls the Mariental a limestone parcel and its tasting line names slate; the house says lean, chalky soil, which the record keeps, and no source here supports slate.
The library's holdings spell Marienthal; the house and Falstaff spell Mariental, which the record uses.
The appellation is given as Burgenland: dry wines of Rust may carry Leithaberg DAC, and whether recent Mariental labels do was not confirmed.

Left out for want of a second source: the namesake's taking over in 1971 and the longer cask time from 2000 (wein.plus only), a fermentation in steel with wild yeast (one merchant), and the family's presence in Rust since 1691 (one source).

The grower behind the 1986, the house's namesake, is taken to be living (no death was found) and is not named in prose; for people.json, his sons Herbert and Gerhard Triebaumer, who have run the estate since 2001 by wein.plus, are living. The couple who sold the plot are named on the house's page but not here, as no dates were found.

changed: wine.sites, wine.label, table, story, cards[1]: the Mariental's soil is lean limestone, as the house's own page says, no longer lean and chalky; the glass keeps a stony edge without chalk.

wine.sites, story, others: the Oberer Wald is the family's inherited site whose rows run north to south, giving a cooler, slimmer wine, as the house's own page says; its more clay and its place beside the Mariental are cut, found in no source of this check.

wine.making, table, story, traps, questions[0]: the barrels of about three hundred litres, most of them new, are cut; Falstaff gives twenty two months in small wooden barrels for 2022 and in oak for 2019, and twenty four months in barrels of five hundred litres for 2018, a Swiss merchant twenty four months in barriques, and no source of this check says the oak is new, so the record says close to two years in small oak barrels and the key says the same.
sources: Falstaff's entry for the 2022 Mariental replaces the merchant's product sheet, as it gives the barrels and the months.
open: Whether the barrels are new is not settled, and with it whether the library's line of no heavy oak is in tension.
The appellation is given as Burgenland; Falstaff lists the 2022 as Blaufränkisch Rust Ried Mariental, and whether recent labels carry Leithaberg DAC was not settled.
The house's namesake is living by every source of this check, so the house keeps its name and the man is never named in prose.

records.place: Schützen am Gebirge, on the Leithaberg west of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Goldberg
wine.sites: The Goldberg above Schützen am Gebirge, on the slope of the Leitha hills: mica schist under clayey loam, its glittering flecks the gold of the name, as the house tells it. Schist warms quickly, so the Goldberg ripens warmer than the cooler limestone Marienthal.
wine.making: Aged for about two years in wood before bottling. For the 2022 the house's own sheet gives the detail: fermentation in open vats with the cap punched down by hand, some three weeks of skin contact, then twenty six months in large casks.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackberry and sloe with cracked pepper and a savoury note of dried herbs, over something cool and stony; the tannin firm and finely grained, the acidity fresh, the finish long and savoury.
wine.ageing: Its youthful firmness eases after five to eight years, and a warm vintage will go twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; open a young bottle into a decanter an hour or two ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the Leitha hills west of the lake; its red, Blaufränkisch led, counts from the 2008 vintage.
Ried marks a single vineyard: this one lies above Schützen am Gebirge, on mica schist, and is recorded since 1555.

records.table: Mica schist lies under Prieler's Blaufränkisch Ried Goldberg, above Schützen am Gebirge on the slope of the Leithaberg, and the glitter of the mica is the gold in its name. After about two years in wood it shows black cherry and pepper over firm tannin.
records.story: The Prieler family's roots in Schützen am Gebirge, on the western side of the Neusiedlersee, run deep: the house says the family appears in the village's records as early as 1347, and the Goldberg, the slope of mica schist above the village, is named in documents of 1555. A grandfather of the family, the house recounts, first put its wine into bottles, and in 1972 the next generation gave the mixed farm over wholly to wine, with Blaufränkisch and the Pinot grapes at its heart, as two importers' histories tell it. Schist warms easily in the sun, the house explains, so the Goldberg ripens warmer than the family's Marienthal on limestone, and the pair show how one grape answers two rocks. Leithaberg DAC came into force in 2010, its reds Blaufränkisch led and counted from the 2008 vintage, and the Goldberg has since come to carry Leithaberg DAC and Ried Goldberg on its label. Beside them the family bottles the Haidsatz, limestone over schist, as a Pinot Blanc of one vineyard. Set the Goldberg against a Blaufränkisch from limestone and the schist shows in a wine that is darker, more peppery and firm.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Leithaberg DAC Ried Marienthal
others.note: From the cooler Marienthal at Oggau, on limestone, the counterpart to the Goldberg's schist.

others.name: Pinot Blanc Leithaberg DAC Ried Haidsatz
others.note: The house's white of one vineyard, Weissburgunder from limestone over schist.

traps: Schützen am Gebirge lies on the Leithaberg, west of the lake; Deutsch Schützen is a village of the Eisenberg in the far south.
The gold of the Goldberg is, in the house's words, the glitter of mica in its schist, not a golden wine.

cards.front: Prieler: when did the family turn its mixed farm wholly over to wine, and to which grapes above all?
cards.back: In 1972, with Blaufränkisch and the Pinot grapes at its heart, as two importers' histories tell it.

cards.front: In what year is the Goldberg above Schützen am Gebirge first named in documents?

questions.q: Prieler's Blaufränkisch Ried Goldberg ripens warmer than the family's Marienthal. What reason does the house give?
opts: Mica schist that warms quickly in the sun
A share of Zweigelt in the blend
Longer ageing in new barriques
Grapes dried on reed mats first
questions.exp: The house says schist warms easily, so the Goldberg ripens warmer than the cooler Marienthal on limestone; the wine is Blaufränkisch, with no Zweigelt, and its grapes are never dried.

questions.q: The house says the Prieler family appears in the records of Schützen am Gebirge from which century?
opts: The fourteenth century
The seventeenth century
The nineteenth century
The twentieth century
questions.exp: The family is named in the village's records in 1347, by the house's account; the Goldberg itself is named in documents of 1555, in the sixteenth century.

sources.title: Prieler: the family and the estate

report: The house is not in the library: 1347, the grandfather's first bottling, the Goldberg's record of 1555, its mica schist and the making rest on the house's own pages (1555 also on Smart Wines), and 1972 on two importers (Skurnik, Perrine's).

The vessel differs by source: Falstaff gives barrique for one vintage and the house's own sheet for 2022 gives twenty six months in large casks; the record follows the house and says about two years in wood.
Left out for want of a second source: a single vineyard Goldberg bottled as early as the 1920s (Skurnik only) and a Goldberg made only in the warmest years (one press piece).
Older vintages were labelled Burgenland (wein.plus lists a 2011 as Blaufränkisch Goldberg Burgenland); the appellation given is Leithaberg DAC, which recent vintages carry.
Living and not named, for people.json: the parents of 1972, Engelbert and Irmgard Prieler, and their children, Silvia and Georg Prieler.
The region record's line (Leithaberg DAC Blaufränkisch from the Goldberg's schist, fine and mineral) agrees with the record.

changed: wine.label: Leithaberg DAC's red is Blaufränkisch led, counted from the 2008 vintage, no longer at least 85 per cent Blaufränkisch, a figure no source of this check gave.
story: the Leithaberg did not become a DAC in 2008; Austrian Wine dates the DAC from 1 September 2010, its whites from the 2009 vintage and its reds from 2008, and the story now says so.

story: the present grower's grandfather and parents, a present tense, become a grandfather of the family and the next generation, who in 1972 gave the mixed farm over wholly to wine with Blaufränkisch and the Pinot grapes at its heart, as Skurnik's history gives it, no longer turned the estate towards quality.

others: the Marienthal is placed at Oggau on limestone, as the house's own sites page gives its steep Oggau part; the Johanneshöhe is cut, since its place (Oggau or the Leithaberg's slopes), its soil and its casks each rest on one secondary source, and the sources of this check disagree on where it lies.
traps: the Goldberg of Deutschkreutz is cut, since no source of this check found such a site.
sources: Austrian Wine's Leithaberg DAC page replaces a Falstaff vintage entry, as it carries the DAC's dates.
open: The making of the 2022, open vats punched down by hand, about three weeks on the skins and twenty six months in large casks, rests on the house's own sheet as the author read it; this check's search of the house's domain did not find it, nor anything against it.
The clayey loam over the Goldberg's schist rests on the author's reading of the house's sites page.

Prieler's Marienthal at Oggau and Ernst Triebaumer's Mariental at Rust may be one site under two spellings; the house says its parcels lie in the steep Oggau part of the Marienthal, which suggests the site runs on into Rust. Not settled, so neither record says so.
